#| label: setup
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(ggplot2); library(kableExtra)
library(patchwork); library(scales)

DATA <- file.path("..", "data")
rd <- function(f) suppressMessages(read_csv(file.path(DATA, f), show_col_types = FALSE))

# Fill in columns a CSV predates, as NA, so a file measured before a field existed still loads
# and the affected numbers read as missing rather than bringing the whole render down.
ensure <- function(df, ...) {
  for (nm in c(...)) if (!nm %in% names(df)) df[[nm]] <- NA_real_
  df
}

# UO palette, as in the companion papers. Green = the linear reference, gold = the
# nonlinearity; amber and blue are held for the model families in Experiments 2-3.
UO <- c(green = "#154733", green2 = "#007030", gold = "#F0B323",
        amber = "#875E00", blue = "#005581", grey = "#6E6E6E")
ACT_COL <- c(identity = UO[["green2"]], relu = UO[["gold"]])
ACT_LAB <- c(identity = "linear", relu = "ReLU")

theme_paper <- function(base = 9) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base) +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.25, color = "grey88"),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = base),
          legend.position = "top", legend.margin = margin(0, 0, -4, 0),
          legend.key.height = unit(9, "pt"),
          axis.title = element_text(size = base))
}

# ---- Experiment 1: the artificial-language grid ----
# 7,560 runs, measured with unified_split -- the SAME function and arguments Experiment 2
# uses. The two independent estimates are two even-sized splits of the observations for each item in each class, so there is
# no alignment step and no projection. Capacity is a reported variable, never a filter.
toy <- rd("artificial_language_grid.csv") |>
  ensure("obs_size_interaction", "size_interaction_null_lo", "size_interaction_null_hi",
         "obs_size_class", "size_class_null_lo", "size_class_null_med", "size_class_null_hi") |>
  mutate(act = factor(activation, c("identity", "relu"), c("linear", "ReLU")),
         # An orthogonality reading means nothing on its own, so each overlap is carried
         # alongside the upper tail of its own null: the largest value an arbitrary orientation
         # produces in 97.5% of draws, from rotating the target subspace 200 times.
         null_hi = leak_item_into_class_null_hi,
         null_lo = leak_item_into_class_null_lo,
         null_med = leak_item_into_class_null_med,
         null_int = leak_int_into_margins_null_hi,
         null_int_lo = leak_int_into_margins_null_lo,
         null_int_med = leak_int_into_margins_null_med)

# The linear arm is a negative control by ALGEBRA, not by stipulation: with additive inputs a
# linear map gives means of the form A(f)+B(c), whose interaction is identically zero
# however much the language contains. Whatever it reports is the measure's own noise, read at
# that exact width, sample size and context level.
toy_null <- toy |> group_by(act, planted = w_int > 0) |>
  summarize(n = n(), med = median(size_interaction),
            p95 = quantile(size_interaction, .95),
            flagged = mean(sig_interaction), .groups = "drop")

# Does the measured interaction track the planted one? Binned, because the achieved share is
# continuous (neither the softmax nor the normalization is linear in the weights).
toy_track <- toy |> filter(w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  mutate(bin = cut(ach_int, c(-Inf, .005, .05, .15, .30, .55, Inf),
                   labels = c("none", ".005-.05", ".05-.15", ".15-.30", ".30-.55", ">.55"))) |>
  group_by(act, bin) |>
  summarize(n = n(), ach = median(ach_int), size_int = median(size_interaction),
            lo = quantile(size_interaction, .25), hi = quantile(size_interaction, .75),
            flagged = mean(sig_interaction), .groups = "drop")

# The same relationship, kept separate by width. Pooled over widths the level is dominated by
# the narrowest models, which cannot build an interaction at all, so the pooled curve
# understates how well the wider ones track. The linear arm is flat at every width, so it is
# summarized once and drawn as a single reference.
toy_track_w <- toy |> filter(w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  mutate(bin = cut(ach_int, c(-Inf, .005, .05, .15, .30, .55, Inf))) |>
  group_by(act, d, bin) |>
  summarize(ach = median(ach_int), size_int = median(size_interaction), .groups = "drop")
toy_track_lin <- toy_track_w |> filter(act == "linear") |>
  group_by(bin) |>
  summarize(ach = median(ach), size_int = median(size_int), .groups = "drop")

# Capacity: below 1 every component can have its own axis, above 1 they cannot.
# One overlap for a table: the value, how many times its own null's median it is, and how many of
# the measurements fall outside that null's 95% interval. The multiple is what makes overlaps
# comparable across widths, since the null moves by orders of magnitude with d; the count is what
# says the effect holds rather than resting on one measurement. Both tables use this, so they
# report the same three things and differ only in what a row is and how many measurements it holds.
ov <- function(v, med, lo, hi, digits = 3) {
  m <- median(v, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (is.na(m)) return("---")
  ratio <- m / median(med, na.rm = TRUE)
  out <- sum(!is.na(v) & (v > hi | v < lo))
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f  (%.1f×, %d/%d)"), m, ratio, out, sum(!is.na(v)))
}

# One size for a table: the share, and how many measurements fall outside its own permutation
# distribution. `obs`, `lo` and `hi` are on the raw scale the draws are on, which is why the raw
# observed value is stored alongside the share; the share alone cannot be compared with them.
# A multiple of the median is given only for the class effect. The item and interaction nulls are
# cross-split products centred on zero, so a ratio to their median is meaningless, while the class
# null is a squared length sitting on a positive floor and a multiple of it reads sensibly.
sz <- function(share, obs, lo, hi, med = NULL, digits = 3) {
  m <- median(share, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (is.na(m)) return("---")
  n <- sum(!is.na(obs))
  if (n == 0) return(sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), m))   # nulls not measured yet
  out <- sum(!is.na(obs) & (obs > hi | obs < lo))
  if (is.null(med) || all(is.na(med)) || median(med, na.rm = TRUE) <= 0)
    return(sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f  (%d/%d)"), m, out, n))
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f  (%.1f×, %d/%d)"),
          m, median(obs, na.rm = TRUE) / median(med, na.rm = TRUE), out, n)
}

# "4 of 6", or "NA" before the nulls are measured, for use in prose.
outof <- function(constr, stem) {
  v <- llm_deep[[paste0(stem, "_outside")]][llm_deep$construction == constr]
  if (!length(v) || all(is.na(v))) return("NA")
  sprintf("%d of %d", sum(v %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE")), sum(!is.na(v)))
}

# How many times its own null's median an effect is. Where every construction clears its null,
# this is what separates them: clearing a floor and standing well clear of it are different facts.
xnull <- function(constr, stem, digits = 1) {
  keep <- llm_deep$construction == constr
  obs <- llm_deep[[paste0("obs_", stem)]][keep]
  med <- llm_deep[[paste0(stem, "_null_med")]][keep]
  if (!length(obs) || all(is.na(obs)) || all(is.na(med))) return("NA")
  m <- median(med, na.rm = TRUE)
  if (is.na(m) || m <= 0) return("NA")
  sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), median(obs, na.rm = TRUE) / m)
}

toy_cap <- toy |> filter(w_int > 0, w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  group_by(act, capacity) |>
  # Formatted here rather than in the table, because `ov` needs the runs themselves to count how
  # many fall outside their null; a summarized row no longer has them.
  summarize(n = n(), size_int = median(size_interaction),
            sz_int = sz(size_interaction, obs_size_interaction,
                        size_interaction_null_lo, size_interaction_null_hi, digits = 3),
            ov_item = ov(leak_item_into_class, null_med, null_lo, null_hi, 4),
            ov_int = ov(leak_int_into_margins, null_int_med, null_int_lo, null_int, 3),
            overlap = median(leak_item_into_class, na.rm = TRUE),
            floor = median(null_hi, na.rm = TRUE),
            ratio = median(leak_item_into_class / null_hi, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

# Context is the nuisance dial: how much of the target is about something other than the item,
# the class and their conjunction. The high end is the regime Experiment 2 sits in.
toy_noise <- toy |> filter(w_int > 0, w_item > 0, w_class > 0) |>
  mutate(cbin = cut(ach_ctx, c(-Inf, .2, .5, .8, Inf),
                    labels = c("<20%", "20-50%", "50-80%", ">80%"))) |>
  group_by(act, cbin) |>
  summarize(n = n(), size_int = median(size_interaction),
            flagged = mean(sig_interaction), .groups = "drop")

g <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
cm <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")

# Short display names for the three constructions. The data keeps the long ones, which the prose
# and the inline expressions index by.
SHORT <- c("POS (noun/verb)"               = "part of speech",
           "role (subject/object)"         = "grammatical role",
           "metaphor (literal/figurative)" = "metaphor")
shortname <- function(x) unname(SHORT[as.character(x)])
nullget <- function(a, pl, col) toy_null[[col]][toy_null$act == a & toy_null$planted == pl]
capget <- function(a, cap, col) toy_cap[[col]][toy_cap$act == a & toy_cap$capacity == cap]

# ---- Experiment 2: language model representations ----
grid_stats <- rd("methods_grid_stats.csv")
gs <- function(constr, col) {
  v <- grid_stats[[col]][grid_stats$construction == constr]
  # median(numeric(0)) is NA, so a construction missing from the stats file used to reach the
  # rendered PDF as a silent "NA". Refuse to render instead.
  if (!length(v)) stop("methods_grid_stats.csv has no rows for construction '", constr,
                       "'; regenerate it with scripts/llm/dataset_stats.py (--vua-dir is ",
                       "required for metaphor)", call. = FALSE)
  if (is.numeric(v)) round(median(v)) else v[1]
}

# Deepest-layer medians, so the prose cannot drift from the table: every figure quoted in the
# text is read from here rather than typed in. `ld` is the median across models.
llm_deep <- NULL   # filled once `llm` exists, below
ld <- function(constr, col) median(llm_deep[[col]][llm_deep$construction == constr], na.rm = TRUE)
# Same, at the embedding layer, and a range of either across the three constructions. Both read
# NA through rather than erroring, so a column the CSVs predate degrades to a blank in the text.
l0 <- function(constr, col) median(llm[[col]][llm$construction == constr & llm$layer == 0],
                                   na.rm = TRUE)
# A size as a share of the whole representation rather than of the grid: the grid's share of the
# total, times the component's share of the grid.
tot <- function(constr, col) ld(constr, col) * ld(constr, "between_adj")

rng <- function(f, col, digits = 2) {
  v <- vapply(levels(llm_deep$construction), function(k) f(k, col), numeric(1))
  if (all(is.na(v))) return("NA")
  paste0(g(min(v, na.rm = TRUE), digits), " to ", g(max(v, na.rm = TRUE), digits))
}

# Experiment 1: What a Learner Builds from a Known Language {#sec-exp1}

The goal of experiment 1 is to validate our measurement on an artificial language whose structure we control as well as examine how a learner represents that structure.

## Dataset {#sec-exp1-data}

In order to examine the representation of linguistic concepts, we constructed an artificial language which comprises a probability distribution over a vocabulary of `r cm(600)` tokens. Every observation is a combination of a **form** (one of `r max(toy$n_form)`), a **class** (one of `r max(toy$n_class)`), and a **context** (drawn from a pool of 400). The motivation for this setup is to give each word a naturalistic environment: the word occurs in a context that favors a specific class-membership (e.g., *walk* as a verb occurs in a different context than *walk* as a noun). Each form is observed `r max(toy$n_obs)` times in each class, every time in a different context, which is what a word in a corpus looks like: one type, many occurrences, each in different company. Consider *walk* used as a verb, in one of those contexts. Four things determine the distribution over the next token. *Walk* itself contributes the same amount whichever class it is used as, and the verb class also contributes the same amount for every verb. The third contribution is comprised of the parts of the representation specific to *walk*-as-a-verb over and above those two: every form and every class has its own random vector, and this term multiplies *walk*'s by the verb's, entry by entry. A sum could be pulled back apart into a form part and a class part; a product cannot, which is what makes this term genuinely joint. The context contributes the rest, which is noise as far as our question goes, though the model still has to encode it exactly as a language model has to encode the rest of a sentence. The four are weighted, summed and passed through a softmax:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&P(\text{next token} \mid f, c, x) = \\
&\quad \operatorname{softmax}\Big( s\big[\, w_\alpha\,\text{item}(f)
  + w_\beta\,\text{class}(c) \\
&\qquad + w_\gamma\,\text{int}(f,c)
  + w_{\text{ctx}}\,\text{context}(x) \,\big] \Big)
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-toy}

Each term is scaled to unit length before it is weighted, so changing the weights changes the mix of the three effects without changing how much signal there is in total, and the task stays equally hard everywhere in the grid.

The weights $w_\alpha$, $w_\beta$ and $w_\gamma$ in @eq-toy control how much of the true distribution each of the three effects contribute, and we cross them factorially over $\{0, 0.5, 1, 2\}$: zero removes an effect from the language altogether, and the other three values make an effect half as strong as another, equal to it, or twice it. Similarly, $w_{\text{ctx}}$ governs how much the context contributes, so we cross those languages with three context weights, ranging from context being a minor part of the true distribution to the dominant one. We train a model on each of the resulting languages at hidden widths of `r paste(sort(unique(toy$d)), collapse = ", ")`, with either a linear or a ReLU activation (@sec-exp1-method). The whole grid is then run with five random seeds, each redrawing the language and reinitializing the model, giving `r format(nrow(toy), big.mark = ",")` runs in all, of which `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(toy$converged))` trained to a loss plateau.

It is worth noting that entanglement is guaranteed under a specific subset of the languages. That is, the structure needs `r max(toy$rank)` dimensions, so its ratio to the hidden width, which we call **capacity**, runs from `r g(min(toy$capacity), 3)` to `r g(max(toy$capacity), 1)`. Below one there is room to give every component its own axis, so any entanglement was chosen; above one there are more components than dimensions to put them in, so they cannot all have their own axis and entanglement is forced [@elhage2022superposition].

## Method {#sec-exp1-method}

### The learner

The input to the learner model comprises three pieces of information: the form, the class, and the context. Each has its own embedding, and the three are concatenated and passed to a standard multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a single hidden layer of width $d$ and either a linear or a ReLU activation function, which outputs a distribution over the vocabulary (@fig-training). The training objective is thus to minimize cross-entropy between the model's predicted distribution over the vocabulary and the true distribution.

![What the learner sees. Every form is observed 24 times at each class, each time in a different context; that variation across contexts is what the measurement later splits in two.](fig-training.pdf){#fig-training width="100%" fig-env="figure*"}

### Decomposing a representation {#sec-measure}

We measure separability by decomposing a word-in-context representation into its lexical representation, its class representation, and its idiosyncratic representation. The representation is the MLP's hidden layer, which for a given form and class varies across the contexts it is observed in, so let $M[i,c] \in \mathbb{R}^d$ be the mean of those hidden states for item $i$ used at class $c$. We decompose that grid by centering, so that

$$
M[i,c] \;=\; \mu + \alpha(i) + \beta(c) + \gamma(i,c),
$$ {#eq-decomp}

where $\mu$ is the grand mean; $\alpha(i)$, item $i$'s mean across classes minus $\mu$, carries the lexical information; $\beta(c)$, the mean across items at class $c$ minus $\mu$, carries the class information; and $\gamma(i,c)$ carries the idiosyncratic information, what item $i$ at class $c$ holds that neither marginal accounts for (@fig-measurement). Because every item is observed in every class with equal weight, neither marginal absorbs part of the other. The four terms add back to $M[i,c]$ exactly, and no two of them vary together across the grid, so their squared lengths sum to the total and we report each as a share of it.

Each of these averages is taken over finitely many observations, which differ only in context, so each carries some of the context term of @eq-toy as noise. We remove it by dividing the observations behind each average into two even-sized splits, running the decomposition on each split separately, and estimating each component's size as the dot product of its two half-estimates, which is large when the splits agree about the component and near zero when they do not. It is the contexts that are divided and not the words, so every word appears in both splits, and the dot product compares two estimates of the same word built from different sentences: noise that differs between the splits is independent and cancels.

For each representation we report two measurements. The first measures the fraction of the representation accounted for by lexical, class and idiosyncratic information: each component's squared length, summed over its vectors and divided by the total, so that the three fractions sum to one. The second measures whether those components occupy the same directions. In order to do so, we project the item vectors onto the class direction and record the fraction of their squared length that survives, and we project the interaction onto the smallest subspace containing both the item and the class vectors (i.e., the span of the two subspaces). A representation is separable if a word's representation is the sum of an item part and a class part with the two on their own axes, so it fails either when the components are non-orthogonal, so that projecting out the class also removes item information, or when there is a third component that is neither an item part nor a class part, whatever its orientation. The question is accordingly not whether class information is present, but how it is carried: on a single direction shared across words, or on a separate direction for each of them.

To quantify whether the effect of size is meaningful, we test each against zero. Size is estimated by taking the dot product of two independent half-estimates of the same component, so noise that differs between the halves cancels out and its value is zero in expectation when the component is absent, which is what makes zero the null. We repeat the measurement over two hundred re-samplings to estimate how much the size varies with which observations fall in which half, and we call a size meaningful when its confidence interval excludes zero. On representations with a component planted at exactly zero, this flags an effect about 5% of the time (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate}), the false-positive rate expected of a 95% confidence interval.

In order to quantify whether the overlap is meaningful, we measure the overlap an effect has with a random subspace. We do so by holding the effect exactly as measured and projecting it onto a random subspace of the same rank, two hundred times, which leaves the effect untouched and varies only the subspace. These two hundred projections give us a distribution of overlaps that an unrelated subspace would yield. An effect lower than this baseline indicates meaningful orthogonality; an effect larger than it indicates meaningful non-orthogonality. We present each overlap as a multiple of the median of this distribution, together with how many measurements fall outside its 95% interval. This gives both the size of the effect and how consistently it holds across measurements.

![If a word's representation were an item part plus a class part, three corners of a $2 \times 2$ grid of means would fix the fourth and the parallelogram would close. It does not. $\gamma$ is how far the actual mean sits from where that additive account puts it, and it is not error: the four components exhaust the grid exactly, so $\gamma$ is the part that belongs to the pairing of a particular word with a particular class. The arrow's length is $\lVert \gamma(i,c) \rVert$, and with two items and two classes it is the whole interaction, since $\gamma$ then has a single degree of freedom and the four means share one vector up to sign. What we report is each component's squared length as a share of the structure across the grid.](fig-measurement.pdf){#fig-measurement width="100%"}

## Results {#sec-exp1-results}

The weights in @eq-toy describe the true distribution the model is trained to match, while the measure reads the representation it builds, so their numbers do not match: a learner handed a language that is 85% interaction can build a representation in which the interaction is a far smaller share, because the representation only has to be enough to produce the answer. Validation asks that the measure track what was planted, read zero when zero was planted, and have a known floor. Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate} reports the separate check in which the components are planted directly in a representation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-toy
#| fig-env: figure*
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "What the artificial-language grid settles about the measure and about the learner, over all 7,560 runs. Left: the measured interaction against the amount planted in the language, one line per hidden width, with the linear condition dashed. The linear condition cannot represent an interaction whatever the language contains and reads zero at every width; under ReLU the measured share rises with the planted one, and the wider the representation the more of it is expressed. The two axes are not on a common scale: the planted share is a share of the target distribution and the measured share is a share of the representation the model builds, and Appendix \\ref{sec-appendix-validate} shows the measure recovers a planted share exactly when the planting is done in a representation. Right: overlap between the item and class effects against capacity, with the dashed line marking the upper end of the null for an arbitrarily oriented effect. Below capacity the two effects are more orthogonal than chance; once dimension counting makes separation impossible they are several times chance. Note the log axis, and that the floor moves by a factor of eight across these widths."
ACT2 <- c(linear = UO[["green2"]], ReLU = UO[["gold"]])
# One ReLU line per width, shading gold to amber with increasing width. Pooled, the level was
# set by the narrowest models, which cannot build an interaction at all.
WID <- colorRampPalette(c(UO[["gold"]], UO[["amber"]]))(length(unique(toy_track_w$d)))
names(WID) <- sort(unique(toy_track_w$d))
pA <- ggplot(filter(toy_track_w, act == "ReLU"), aes(ach, size_int, color = factor(d))) +
  geom_line(data = toy_track_lin, mapping = aes(ach, size_int), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = ACT2[["linear"]], linetype = 2, linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .6) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = WID, name = "width") +
  labs(x = "interaction planted in the language", y = "interaction measured\nin the representation") +
  theme_paper(8)

# one chance line, not one per condition: the two differ slightly because the class subspace
# rank is estimated, and drawing both makes a zigzag that reads as structure when it is not
floor_line <- toy_cap |> group_by(capacity) |> summarize(floor = median(floor), .groups = "drop")
pB <- ggplot(toy_cap, aes(capacity, overlap, color = act)) +
  geom_line(data = floor_line, mapping = aes(capacity, floor), inherit.aes = FALSE,
            color = UO[["grey"]], linetype = 2, linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .6) + geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.135, y = 0.032, label = "chance", size = 2.5,
           color = UO[["grey"]], hjust = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ACT2, name = NULL) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(.125, .25, .5, 1, 2)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE)) +
  labs(x = "capacity (structure rank / hidden width)", y = "item-class overlap (log)") +
  theme_paper(8)

# Each panel keeps its own legend: collected, the left panel's width scale and the right
# panel's activation scale sit side by side in the same gold and read as one key.
(pA | pB) &
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.margin = margin(0, 0, -6, 0))
```

The measure reports zero when the answer is zero. Under the linear activation the hidden layer is a weighted sum of the three embeddings, so its interaction is identically zero however much the language contains (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-math}), and every reading the measure gives there is its own noise. Across all `r cm(nullget("linear", TRUE, "n"))` runs where the language *did* contain an interaction, it reports a median share of `r g(nullget("linear", TRUE, "med"), 4)` and flags one in `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * nullget("linear", TRUE, "flagged"))` of them, the nominal rate for a test at the 5% level; where no interaction was planted it flags `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * nullget("linear", FALSE, "flagged"))`. This calibration comes from a condition whose true value is provably zero, measured at every width, sample size and noise level in the grid.

The measure also tracks what is there. Under ReLU the measured interaction rises monotonically with the planted one (@fig-toy, left), and the rate at which it is flagged rises with it, from `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * min(toy_track$flagged[toy_track$act == "ReLU" & toy_track$bin != "none"]))` at the smallest nonzero setting to `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(toy_track$flagged[toy_track$act == "ReLU"]))` at the largest. With no interaction planted, ReLU flags `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * nullget("ReLU", FALSE, "flagged"))` of runs, below nominal: the nonlinearity does not manufacture an interaction out of an additive language. The measured shares are smaller than the planted ones throughout, and the gap is a fact about the representation rather than about the measure: planting the same components directly in a representation recovers them almost exactly in every class (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate}), so a model trained on a language built largely out of the interaction still builds a representation that carries much less of it. How much less depends on how wide the representation is, and what matters here is that the relationship is monotone and that zero maps to zero.

Item and class effects entangle only when there is no room for them not to, and this is the substantive result (@fig-toy, right; @tbl-toy). With capacity well below one, ReLU's item-class overlap is `r g(capget("ReLU", 0.125, "overlap"), 4)` against a chance level of `r g(capget("ReLU", 0.125, "floor"), 4)`, so the two effects are *more* orthogonal than two arbitrary directions would be, which is what a learner that has room and uses it looks like. At capacity 1 the overlap is `r g(capget("ReLU", 1, "overlap"), 3)` against a floor of `r g(capget("ReLU", 1, "floor"), 4)`, about `r g(capget("ReLU", 1, "ratio"), 1)` times chance, and at capacity 2 it is `r g(capget("ReLU", 2, "overlap"), 3)`; the linear condition stays at or below chance throughout. This is superposition in a setting where we can watch it happen: when the number of directions the structure needs exceeds the number available, the components stop being orthogonal because they cannot all be, and nothing about the language changed across those runs.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-toy
#| tbl-cap: "What a learner builds from the same languages as its representation runs out of room. Capacity is the rank the structure needs divided by the hidden width, so the rows run from a width of 128 down to 8 while the languages are held fixed: the median interaction planted is 0.097 in every row, and the fall down the *interaction* column is therefore the width and not the language. *Interaction* is the interaction's share of the representation, a size. The last two columns are orientations, and a separate question: how much of the item effect lies in the class subspace, and how much of the interaction lies in the span of the two main effects. Each is the fraction that survives the projection, which is the quantity that matters, given as the median, then in parentheses how many times its own null's median it is and how many of the runs in that row fall outside that null's 95% interval, over the number of runs in the *runs* column. The null holds the effect fixed and rotates the target subspace at random 200 times. Reporting the multiple rather than the raw fraction is what makes the rows comparable: the null itself moves several-fold down this table as the width falls, so the fractions are not comparable across rows on their own. A value below one is more orthogonal than an arbitrary orientation would be, which with room to spare ReLU is. Table \ref{tbl-llm} reports the same three things for the language models. The linear arm has no interaction to orient, so its last column is empty. Below capacity one a fully separable solution is reachable by dimension counting; above one it is not."
toy_cap |>
  transmute(condition = act, capacity = g(capacity, 3), runs = n,
            interaction = sz_int,
            `item-class overlap` = ov_item,
            # the linear arm has no interaction to orient, so its direction is noise
            `interaction overlap` = ifelse(act == "linear", "---", ov_int)) |>
  arrange(condition, capacity) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrr", linesep = "", escape = FALSE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7)
```

The measure also works when the representation primarily encodes contextual information unrelated to the specific form and class. When the context term accounts for more than 80% of the variance in the logits, leaving under a fifth for the form, the class and their interaction combined, ReLU's measured interaction holds at `r g(toy_noise$size_int[toy_noise$act == "ReLU" & toy_noise$cbin == ">80%"], 3)` against `r g(toy_noise$size_int[toy_noise$act == "ReLU" & toy_noise$cbin == "<20%"], 3)` when context is minor, and the flag rate falls from `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * toy_noise$flagged[toy_noise$act == "ReLU" & toy_noise$cbin == "<20%"])` to `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * toy_noise$flagged[toy_noise$act == "ReLU" & toy_noise$cbin == ">80%"])`. Power degrades, as it must with twenty-four observations per item and class, but the estimate does not drift. That is the regime Experiment 2 sits in, since a word's hidden state varies mostly with the sentence it appears in rather than with the word or its class.

Two things carry into Experiment 2. The instrument reads zero when the answer is zero and tracks the answer when it is not, at the sample size and noise level the language models will be measured at. And whether the item and class effects come out orthogonal is governed by whether the representation had room, which is a fact about capacity rather than about the language, so near-orthogonality in a wide model is uninformative on its own and has to be read against its own chance level.

# Experiment 2: Item and Category in Language Models {#sec-exp2}

Experiment 1 established that a learner fitting an interactive language cannot represent it as item plus class, and that a nonlinearity additionally makes the components non-orthogonal. Experiment 2 applies the same decomposition to the contextual representations of pretrained language models, across three linguistic distinctions chosen to span grammar and meaning.

## Dataset {#sec-exp2-data}

For part of speech and grammatical role we concatenate six general-domain English Universal Dependencies treebanks [@nivre2020ud]: EWT, GUM, LinES, ParTUT, GENTLE and PUD, giving `r cm(41095)` sentences and `r cm(706323)` tokens. A lemma must be attested in both classes often enough to estimate a mean at each, and a single treebank yields too few such lemmas. For metaphor we use the VUA20 corpus [@leong2020vua; @steen2010vua], restricted to content words, which supplies `r cm(gs("metaphor", "n_pre_grid_tokens"))` labeled tokens.

All three constructions are **same-token**: the item's surface form is identical across the two classes, so the representation is read from the same token in both, and no part of any difference can come from tokenization.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-constructions
#| tbl-cap: "The three constructions. All three key the item on the **surface form**, so the token is identical in both classes of the distinction. *Analyzed* counts the forms attested often enough at each level to estimate a mean at each."
tibble::tribble(
  ~distinction,       ~levels,                           ~analyzed,
  "part of speech",   "\\textsc{noun} / \\textsc{verb}",  max(llm$n_items[llm$construction == "POS (noun/verb)"]),
  "grammatical role", "\\textit{nsubj} / \\textit{obj}",  49,
  "metaphor",         "literal / figurative",             gs("metaphor", "n_items_kept")) |>
  mutate(tokens = c(4722, 2150, gs("metaphor", "n_grid_tokens")),
         across(c(analyzed, tokens), \(v) format(v, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE))) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrr", linesep = "", escape = FALSE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8)
```

Keying the item on the *lemma* instead admits more items (`r cm(gs("pos_noun_verb", "n_items_kept"))` rather than `r max(llm$n_items[llm$construction == "POS (noun/verb)"])`, drawn from `r cm(gs("pos_noun_verb", "n_items_eligible"))` lemmas attested as both), but a lemma pools every inflected form: *run* and *runs* as a noun against *run*, *runs*, *ran* and *running* as a verb. Those are different tokens, and the consequence shows up at the embedding layer, which has no context to work with and so can only distinguish classes that differ in their input. Keyed on the lemma the layer-0 interaction is 0.083 to 0.172 across models; keyed on the form it is 0.0010 to 0.0028. The difference is inflection rather than representation, and keying on the form removes it at the cost of a smaller item set. Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-morph} shows what the measure does on a distinction where the property cannot be arranged at all.

**Identifiability.** The interaction $\gamma(i,c)$ is estimable only for an item observed in more than one class, since it is defined by how an item's representation shifts across classes, and we additionally require at least 10 tokens for each item in each class so that a mean can be estimated and then split in two. This restricts the scope for part of speech, where it selects forms genuinely used both ways, such as *run* or *hit*. Role and metaphor carry no such restriction, since any noun occurs as both subject and object and any content word occurs both literally and figuratively, which is one reason they broaden the claim. The median item holds around 24 tokens in each class across the three constructions, the sample size the measure is validated at in Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate}.

We measure two model families at three matched scales: OPT-BabyLM, trained on developmentally plausible quantities of child-available language [@warstadt2023babylm], and Pythia, trained on the Pile [@biderman2023pythia], at 125M/160M, 350M/410M and 1.3B/1.4B parameters, with widths of 768, 1024 and 2048. Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-models} gives parameter counts and training-token estimates.

## Method {#sec-exp2-method}

The decomposition, the two reported quantities and the replication logic are those of @sec-exp1-method. For every token we take the hidden state of the word's **last subword** at every layer, from the embeddings through the final block, aligning subwords to corpus tokens with the tokenizer's word alignment. Sentences are drawn in a fixed random order and processed until roughly 300K tokens are extracted per model, so all models see the same material, and representations are extracted once with every analysis running offline from them.

The two independent estimates come from the corpus itself: each item in a class is a word used across many sentences, so we divide its token contexts into two disjoint, even-sized splits and estimate the grid from each. What cancels is context noise, the variation in a word's hidden state across the sentences it appears in, which is the same thing the split cancels in Experiment 1.

**Standardization.** Transformer hidden states contain a few *rogue* dimensions whose variance exceeds the rest by two to three orders of magnitude [@timkey2021bark], and these would otherwise dominate any subspace estimated from the raw scatter, so we divide each dimension by its standard deviation before decomposing. This is a diagonal rescaling rather than a whitening, so it needs no favorable ratio of samples to dimensions; the measure is accordingly invariant to per-dimension rescaling but not to arbitrary linear reparameterization, which we return to in Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-math}.

## Results {#sec-exp2-results}

```{r}
#| label: fig-llm
#| fig-env: figure*
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 3.7
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "How the three components grow through the network, for every model and every distinction. Relative depth runs from the static embedding layer (0) to the final block (1). Top: the interaction's share of representational structure. Middle: the class effect's share. Bottom: the portable fraction, the class effect's share of the two together, which is the quantity the three distinctions are ordered by. Each line is one model; color distinguishes the two training corpora. Both components are built by depth, and the interaction is the larger of the two throughout. The deepest-layer values, with their chance levels, are in Table \\ref{tbl-llm}."
plt <- llm |>
  mutate(portable = size_class / (size_class + size_int)) |>
  select(construction, family, size, depth, size_int, size_class, portable) |>
  pivot_longer(c(size_int, size_class, portable), names_to = "component",
               values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, c("size_int", "size_class", "portable"),
                            c("interaction", "class effect", "portable fraction")))
ggplot(plt, aes(depth, share, color = family, group = interaction(family, size))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .55, alpha = .85) +
  facet_grid(component ~ construction, scales = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(BabyLM = UO[["gold"]], Pythia = UO[["blue"]]), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .5, 1)) +
  labs(x = "relative depth", y = NULL) +
  theme_paper(8) + theme(strip.placement = "outside")
```

The two main effects sit on separate axes. At the deepest layer, item-class overlap runs `r g(0.0032, 4)` to `r g(0.0067, 4)` for part of speech and `r g(0.0025, 4)` to `r g(0.0062, 4)` for grammatical role, so projecting out the class direction leaves better than 99% of the item effect intact. Both sit above the upper end of their null, so the residual alignment is real rather than a by-product of the dimension count, but it is small enough that these representations do not achieve class structure by borrowing the directions that carry word identity. Where a shared class direction exists, it is its own direction.

The interaction, however, does not have axes of its own, and this is what decides whether a third component could simply be added to the description and separability recovered in a wider sense. For part of speech `r g(ld("POS (noun/verb)", "leak_int"), 3)` of the interaction lies in the span of the two main effects, for role `r g(ld("role (subject/object)", "leak_int"), 3)` and for metaphor `r g(ld("metaphor (literal/figurative)", "leak_int"), 3)`, against nulls whose upper ends are `r g(ld("POS (noun/verb)", "leak_int_null"), 3)`, `r g(ld("role (subject/object)", "leak_int_null"), 3)` and `r g(ld("metaphor (literal/figurative)", "leak_int_null"), 3)` (@tbl-llm). The partition of the grid says nothing about direction, so these numbers are not implied by the decomposition: the item-by-class term reuses the very directions that carry item identity and class membership. Read with the first overlap, they say something more specific than "not separable". The failure is not that item and class have been collapsed onto shared axes, since those remain distinct; it is that the part of class structure specific to each word is written in the same directions as everything else. For metaphor the question does not arise, because the class effect never rises above the level at which an orientation is worth reporting, which is itself the first indication of how little of metaphoricity is carried by a shared direction. It is not, however, absent. Against its own permutation distribution the class effect falls outside the 95% interval in `r outof("metaphor (literal/figurative)", "size_class")` models, so metaphoricity does have a direction shared across words; it is simply a very small one. What separates the three constructions is not whether they clear their permutation distributions, which all of them do, but by how much: the class effect is `r xnull("POS (noun/verb)", "size_class")` times its null's median for part of speech and `r xnull("role (subject/object)", "size_class")` times for grammatical role, against `r xnull("metaphor (literal/figurative)", "size_class")` times for metaphor (@tbl-llm). A class effect this small is exactly the case a size cannot settle on its own, since a squared length sits above a floor set by how many observations went into it, and the permutation is what distinguishes a small effect from no effect.

A substantial interaction is there, and depth builds it. In all three distinctions the interaction is essentially absent at layer 0, between 0.0002 and 0.0051 across every construction and model, and rises monotonically with depth to between 0.023 and 0.246 (@fig-llm, top row). Because the item is keyed on the surface form, the token is identical in both classes, so the static embedding layer has nothing to distinguish them with, and it does not. Everything the measure finds is therefore created by contextualization rather than inherited from the input, and it is not positional: zeroing OPT-BabyLM's absolute position embeddings leaves the class structure more word-specific rather than less (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-positions}). This is the component that breaks separability, since it is neither a fact about the word nor a fact about the class.

All three sizes are shares of the grid, and the grid has already averaged away how a word varies across the contexts it appears in, so how much of the representation the grid is in the first place is worth stating. At the embedding layer it is `r rng(l0, "between_adj")` of the variance across the three constructions, which is the same-token design working as intended: identical tokens differ little before anything contextualizes them. At the deepest layer it is `r rng(ld, "between_adj")`, so most of what the model computes there is about the sentence a word is in rather than about the word and its class. Multiplying the two through, the deepest-layer item effect for part of speech is `r g(tot("POS (noun/verb)", "size_item"), 2)` of the representation rather than the `r g(ld("POS (noun/verb)", "size_item"), 2)` it is of the grid, and the class effect and interaction scale down in the same proportion, with context taking the remainder. Both figures are corrected for the noise each grid entry carries as an average over finitely many observations, which otherwise inflates the grid's apparent share by an amount that shrinks as tokens per item grow and so differs across constructions (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-math}).

The class effect grows with depth as well (@fig-llm, middle row), and that matters for the framing. Models are not choosing between abstraction and entanglement; contextualization builds both at once. A description of these representations as either abstract or exemplar-like is therefore underdetermined by the data, and the useful question is not which one they are but what the balance is.

That balance is graded across distinctions. @tbl-llm reports it as the *portable fraction*: of the structure that distinguishes the two classes, how much is a direction shared across words rather than specific to each word. Grammatical role is the most portable at 0.46, part of speech next at 0.31, and metaphor by far the least at 0.07, so only about a fourteenth of metaphor's class-relevant structure is carried by a shared direction. The ordering is worth noting: part of speech has the largest class effect of the three in absolute terms, but also much the largest interaction, so proportionally less of what distinguishes its classes is portable than for grammatical role. Metaphoricity is close to being encoded word by word, and what makes a use of *plant* figurative is largely not what makes a use of *course* figurative.

# Experiment 3: Does the Interaction Carry the Class? {#sec-exp3}

Experiment 2 shows that the interaction is large and that it replicates across independent splits of a word's occurrences, but neither shows what it is *about*. An item-by-class term captures any reliable difference between a word's uses in the two classes, and some of that difference is context correlated with the label rather than the label itself, since metaphorical uses occur in different sentences from literal ones and subjects appear in different constructions from objects. So $\gamma$ is an upper bound on class-binding, and the question is whether any of it is the class.

## Method {#sec-exp3-method}

We test it by decoding. If $\gamma$ encodes the class, the class should be recoverable from the part of a token's representation that is neither the item effect nor the shared class direction, and we remove both explicitly. All decoding happens *within* a single word, so we ask whether *plant*'s figurative uses can be told from *plant*'s literal ones, never whether *plant* can be told from *account*; the item effect is constant within a word and so cannot contribute. We then estimate $\beta$ as the difference between the two class means pooled over all items, normalize it, and remove that component from every token, so that whatever separates the classes afterwards is not the direction they share.

What remains is the interaction: the part of a word-at-a-class that is neither a fact about the word nor a fact about the class. We decode it with a cross-validated logistic probe, five folds, classes balanced by subsampling within each word so that chance is 0.50, and average the resulting accuracies over words, with a word contributing only if it has at least eight tokens in each class. Accuracies are averaged unweighted over words and some words rest on few tokens, so the mean carries a percentile bootstrap interval over words. The whole procedure is then repeated with the class labels permutated within each word, which preserves every word's token count and class balance while destroying the labelling, and that null is where a probe reading its own cross-validation folds would land. We run this at the deepest layer of the largest model in each family, for all three constructions.

## Results {#sec-exp3-results}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-decode
#| tbl-cap: "Class decoded from the interaction, at the deepest layer of the largest model in each family. The item is held fixed and the shared class direction is projected out, so neither the item effect nor the class effect can contribute. *Class* is the accuracy of that decode and *null* permutates class labels within each word; brackets are percentile bootstrap intervals over words. Chance is 0.50."
dec <- bind_rows(
  rd("llm_decode_pos_form.csv") |> mutate(construction = "POS (noun/verb)"),
  rd("llm_decode_interaction.csv") |> filter(construction != "pos") |>
    mutate(construction = recode(construction,
                                 role = "role (subject/object)",
                                 metaphor = "metaphor (literal/figurative)"))) |>
  left_join(MODELS, by = "model") |>
  mutate(construction = factor(construction, c("POS (noun/verb)", "role (subject/object)",
                                               "metaphor (literal/figurative)")))

dec |>
  arrange(construction, family) |>
  transmute(distinction = shortname(construction), family,
            words = n_peritem,
            class = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", class_peritem,
                            class_peritem_lo, class_peritem_hi),
            null = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", class_peritem_null,
                           class_peritem_null_lo, class_peritem_null_hi)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7)
```

The interaction is about the class. In every construction and both families the class is recoverable from the interaction at well above chance while the permutated null sits on chance (@tbl-decode), reaching `r g(dec$class_peritem[dec$construction == "POS (noun/verb)" & dec$family == "Pythia"], 2)` for part of speech, `r g(dec$class_peritem[dec$construction == "role (subject/object)" & dec$family == "Pythia"], 2)` for grammatical role and `r g(dec$class_peritem[dec$construction == "metaphor (literal/figurative)" & dec$family == "Pythia"], 2)` for metaphor, with bootstrap intervals excluding the nulls by a wide margin in all six cases. The null landing on chance is what makes those accuracies interpretable, since it is the same probe, the same folds, the same word-level averaging and the same small per-word samples with only the labelling destroyed.

The effect is graded the same way the interaction's size is. Part of speech decodes best, role next, metaphor least, which is the ordering of the portable fraction in @tbl-llm read backwards: the distinctions whose class-relevant structure is least portable are also the ones whose interaction carries the class least strongly. Two measurements, one geometric and one functional, agree on the same ranking.

Metaphor is the case where this matters most. Its class effect never clears the threshold at which an orientation is worth reporting (@sec-exp2-results), so on the geometric evidence alone one could conclude that metaphoricity is not represented at all, yet it decodes from the interaction at `r g(dec$class_peritem[dec$construction == "metaphor (literal/figurative)" & dec$family == "Pythia"], 2)` against a null of `r g(dec$class_peritem_null[dec$construction == "metaphor (literal/figurative)" & dec$family == "Pythia"], 2)`. It is represented; it is simply not represented as a direction shared across words, and a method that looks only for a shared direction would have missed it.

This result has a definite scope. It shows that $\gamma$ carries the specific label rather than generic correlated context, since generic context would not survive holding the word fixed and removing the shared axis. It does not show that $\gamma$ is *only* the label: context correlated with the class within a word survives both removals, so the interaction remains an upper bound on class-binding, and this raises the floor rather than closing the gap.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

::: {.content-visible when-format="acl-pdf"}
<!-- PLACEHOLDER: author to write. -->
:::

# Limitations {.unnumbered}

Everything here is English, and rests on three distinctions measured in two model families at three scales each. The graded ordering we report is an ordering across *these* distinctions, and whether it holds for aspect, animacy or definiteness is untested.

The measure is invariant to per-dimension rescaling and to rotation, but not to arbitrary linear reparameterization, so overlap between the item and class effects is relative to the model's own basis. We take that to be the basis of interest, since LayerNorm and the feed-forward nonlinearities act coordinate-wise and a downstream output layer operates on the unwhitened space; a reader who wants a fully gauge-free quantity will not find one here. The component sizes, their growth with depth and their significance do not depend on that choice.

Two things we would like to have done. These are endpoint measurements, so they say nothing about the order in which the two components are learned, which needs training checkpoints. And the interaction captures any systematic within-word difference between the classes, so a distinction realized through the contexts a word appears in is measured together with those contexts. For a contextual model we take that to be what representing the distinction consists in, but separating the two would need a construction in which they can be varied independently.
